summary:
Visitors to Hawaii stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the changed treatment to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Document risk is documented rather than theoretical. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. A separate exposure attaches at visa stage: the State Department announced on 5 February 2025 that trans athletes would be barred from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, applicants who list a gender other than their sex assigned at birth are treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds, and flagged applications carry an internal marking.

State-level conditions in Hawaii sit at the protective end of the national range. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii among fifteen states in the Most Protective tier, describing their laws as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Hawaii also operates a healthcare shield, listed on the Movement Advancement Project Transgender Healthcare Equality Map with data current to 27 September 2026 as a state holding a shield law or executive order in 2026. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in Hawaii but banned in the patient's home state, which makes Hawaii directly usable as a care destination by visitors travelling from prohibiting jurisdictions. The same map counts 16 states and the District of Columbia holding shields, covering 38% of trans people aged 13 and over, against 32 states and 5 territories, 56%, holding none.
tangentialFactors:
The protective tier Hawaii sits in is defined against a markedly different floor elsewhere. In the worst-law states the same rubric records prison terms of up to five years in Idaho and arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in Florida, and an April 2025 arrest of a transgender student in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under such a law.

Federal measures affecting visitors remain contested in court. Several of the executive and agency actions on passports, care and facilities have been blocked or enjoined, and the healthcare map notes that some youth-care bans tracked nationally have been permanently blocked, so the operative position can shift between litigation rounds.

Wider turbulence shapes expectations at the border. In April 2025 several foreign governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no state bathroom ban, so a visitor's exposure varies sharply by itinerary even when the federal layer is constant.
localsOnly:
Hawaii's shield reaches residents and providers as well as those who travel in for care: providers delivering care that is legal in Hawaii are protected from civil or criminal charges arising from a patient's home-state prohibition, and patients receiving that care carry the same protection.

The rubric that produced the July 2026 ranking scores youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition. Hawaii's placement in the top tier of fifteen states indicates that none of those restrictions applies within Hawaii, in contrast to states where marker changes are barred or bathroom use is an arrestable offence.

Hawaii's position leaves it among the minority of jurisdictions nationally that combine protective state law with a care shield; 32 states and 5 territories, 56% of the country, provide no shield at all, so residents of those places have no equivalent protection to rely on.
outOfScopeNotes:
The healthcare map groups shield statutes and executive orders in a single category, so the source inventory does not resolve whether Hawaii's shield rests on legislation or on an executive instrument, nor its exact scope or effective date beyond 2026.

No Hawaii-specific material on identity-document rules, birth-certificate or driver-licence marker changes, facilities access, or hate-crime protection appears in the inventory. Those questions are not answered here rather than answered negatively.

The interaction between the federal passport regime and Hawaii's shield is unresolved in the sources: nothing indicates whether a visitor whose federal documents do not match their presentation encounters any different treatment in Hawaii than elsewhere in the United States.

No incidents involving trans visitors in Hawaii are documented in the inventory, and no enforcement or complaint statistics for Hawaii are available here. The national figures quoted for shield coverage are dated 27 September 2026 and the legal-risk ranking July 2026.
